claim: Decapentaplegic (Dpp) is the Drosophila BMP homolog.
source: Decapentaplegic (Dpp), the Drosophila BMP homolog, has served as a paradigm to characterize the role of morphogens in regulating patterning of developing tissues (Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).

claim: Dpp is expressed in a central stripe that corresponds to the anterior-posterior (AP) compartment boundary in the developing Drosophila wing disc.
source: In the developing Drosophila wing disc, Dpp is expressed in a central stripe that corresponds to the anterior-posterior (AP) compartment boundary, and its gradient provides a series of concentration thresholds throughout the tissue that set the transcriptional state of target genes in discrete domains of gene expression as a function of their distance from the source (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996).

claim: The Dpp gradient provides concentration thresholds that set the transcriptional state of target genes in discrete domains as a function of distance from the source.
source: In the developing Drosophila wing disc, Dpp is expressed in a central stripe that corresponds to the anterior-posterior (AP) compartment boundary, and its gradient provides a series of concentration thresholds throughout the tissue that set the transcriptional state of target genes in discrete domains of gene expression as a function of their distance from the source (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996).

claim: Graded activation of MAD and the inverse gradient of Brinker contribute to transcriptional regulation of Dpp target genes in discrete domains.
source: Graded activation of the Dpp transducer MAD and the inverse gradient of Brinker, a transcriptional repressor negatively regulated by Dpp, contribute to the transcriptional regulation of Dpp target genes in discrete domains (Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).

claim: Brinker is a transcriptional repressor negatively regulated by Dpp.
source: Graded activation of the Dpp transducer MAD and the inverse gradient of Brinker, a transcriptional repressor negatively regulated by Dpp, contribute to the transcriptional regulation of Dpp target genes in discrete domains (Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014).

claim: The Dpp gradient participates in specifying cell identities in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Thus, the participation of the Dpp gradient in specifying cell identities in a concentration-dependent manner is well accepted.
evidence: This is stated as an accepted fact in the scientific community.

claim: Proliferative growth is homogenous in the developing wing.
source: By contrast, the role of the Dpp gradient in regulating tissue size has been a topic of intense debate as proliferative growth is homogenous in the developing wing (Milán et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Milán et al., 1996).

claim: The role of the Dpp gradient in regulating tissue size has been a topic of intense debate.
source: By contrast, the role of the Dpp gradient in regulating tissue size has been a topic of intense debate as proliferative growth is homogenous in the developing wing (Milán et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the scientific discourse.

claim: The classical 'steepness model' proposes that juxtaposition of cells sensing disparate levels of morphogen promotes proliferative growth.
source: The classical 'steepness model' proposes that the juxtaposition of cells sensing disparate levels of the morphogen promotes proliferative growth (Lawrence and Struhl, 1996; Rogulja and Irvine, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Lawrence and Struhl, 1996; Rogulja and Irvine, 2005).

claim: The Dpp gradient scales with the size of the wing primordium.
source: This model is questioned by the observation that the Dpp-gradient scales with the size of the wing primordium and that the slope of the gradient does not change (Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Wartlick et al., 2011).

claim: The slope of the Dpp gradient does not change as the wing primordium grows.
source: This model is questioned by the observation that the Dpp-gradient scales with the size of the wing primordium and that the slope of the gradient does not change (Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Wartlick et al., 2011).

claim: The 'temporal rule model' posits that cells divide when Dpp signaling levels have increased by 50%.
source: These same authors propose a new model - the 'temporal rule model' - that posits that cells divide when Dpp signaling levels have increased by 50%.
evidence: This is a description of a model proposed in the literature.

claim: Cells lacking MAD and Brinker activities grow at rates comparable to wild-type cells.
source: However, cells lacking MAD and Brinker activities - in which the increase of Dpp signaling levels is genetically blocked - were shown to grow at rates comparable to those of wild-type cells (Schwank et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Schwank et al., 2012).

claim: The 'growth equalisation model' suggests that Dpp controls growth of the central region of the wing by repressing Brinker.
source: The alternative 'growth equalisation model' suggests that Dpp controls growth of the central region of the wing by repressing Brinker (Schwank et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Schwank et al., 2011).

claim: Dpp emanating from the AP boundary is mainly required for the growth of the center of the wing disc, the region with the highest levels of Dpp activity.
source: The recent use of membrane-tethered-GFP nanobodies against Dpp-GFP to modulate Dpp spreading proposes that Dpp emanating from the AP boundary is mainly required for the growth of the center of the wing disc, the region with the highest levels of Dpp activity (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Harmansa et al., 2015).

claim: Dpp emanating from the AP boundary is not required for wing growth according to CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing studies.
source: A recent report questions the temporal and spatial requirement of Dpp expression and activity in promoting wing growth. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing of the dpp locus combined with the FLP-FRT recombination system to temporally control the removal of Dpp from its endogenous stripe domain has come to the conclusion that Dpp emanating from the AP boundary is not required for wing growth and that the growth-promoting role of Dpp is restricted to the early stages of wing development (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).

claim: The growth-promoting role of Dpp is restricted to the early stages of wing development according to CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing studies.
source: A recent report questions the temporal and spatial requirement of Dpp expression and activity in promoting wing growth. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing of the dpp locus combined with the FLP-FRT recombination system to temporally control the removal of Dpp from its endogenous stripe domain has come to the conclusion that Dpp emanating from the AP boundary is not required for wing growth and that the growth-promoting role of Dpp is restricted to the early stages of wing development (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015).

claim: Dpp emanating from the AP compartment boundary is required throughout development to promote growth of the developing wing appendage.
source: We show that Dpp emanating from the AP compartment boundary is required throughout development to promote growth by regulating cell proliferation and tissue size.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dpp regulates growth and proliferation rates equally in central and lateral regions of the developing wing appendage.
source: Dpp regulates growth and proliferation rates equally in central and lateral regions of the developing wing appendage and reduced levels of Dpp affects similarly the width and length of the resulting wing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced levels of Dpp affects similarly the width and length of the resulting wing.
source: Dpp regulates growth and proliferation rates equally in central and lateral regions of the developing wing appendage and reduced levels of Dpp affects similarly the width and length of the resulting wing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Graded activity of Dpp is not an absolute requirement for wing growth.
source: We also present evidence supporting the proposal that graded activity of Dpp is not an absolute requirement for wing growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All individuals expressing different dpp-RNAi hairpins produced rudimentary wings resembling those caused by classical dpp-disk alleles.
source: All individuals expressing the different dpp-RNAi hairpins produced rudimentary wings resembling those caused by the classical dpp-disk alleles in which the enhancers driving dpp expression to the imaginal tissues are removed [Figure 1A,A'; (Masucci et al., 1990)].
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1A,A' and comparison to published research (Masucci et al., 1990).

claim: dpp-RNAi-expressing wings maintained largely well-formed and grown distal hinge structures.
source: We observed that dpp-RNAi-expressing wings maintained largely well-formed and grown distal hinge structures (eg. alula and costa, Figure 1A), as occurs in dpp-disk wings (Zecca et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1A and comparison to published research (Zecca et al., 1995).

claim: Individuals raised at 18°C with tub-gal80ts showed no overt wing phenotype.
source: Individuals raised at 18°C showed no overt wing phenotype (Figure 1B,B'), while those raised at 25°C showed only a mild growth phenotype (Figure 1C,C').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1B,B'.

claim: Individuals raised at 25°C with tub-gal80ts showed only a mild growth phenotype.
source: Individuals raised at 18°C showed no overt wing phenotype (Figure 1B,B'), while those raised at 25°C showed only a mild growth phenotype (Figure 1C,C').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C,C'.

claim: All individuals raised at 29°C expressing different dpp-RNAi hairpins produced rudimentary wings.
source: All individuals raised at 29°C and expressing the different dpp-RNAi hairpins produced rudimentary wings (Figure 1D,D').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1D,D'.

claim: The developing appendage was drastically reduced in size when raised at 29°C with dpp-RNAi expression.
source: The developing appendage, labelled by the expression of a Nubbin (Nub) antibody, was drastically reduced in size when raised at 29°C (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In dpp-depleted wing primordia, the sizes of the D and V compartments were reduced in a proportional manner.
source: In dpp-depleted wing primordia, the sizes of the D and V compartments were reduced in a proportional manner, which is consistent with the symmetric reduction in size of the D and V surfaces of the adult wing (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The size of the A compartment was reduced to a larger extent than the size of the P compartment in dpp-depleted wing primordia.
source: We observed that the size of the A compartment was reduced to a larger extent than the size of the P compartment (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The size of the wing hinge was largely unaffected by dpp depletion.
source: The size of the wing hinge (the distance between the IR and OR, Figure 1E, bottom panels) was largely unaffected.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: dpp mRNA levels decreased in the developing wing appendage upon dpp-RNAi expression.
source: As expected, dpp mRNA levels and Dpp activity levels, visualised with an antibody against the phosphorylated form of the Dpp transducer MAD (p-MAD) and by the expression of the Dpp target genes spalt and optomotor-blind [omb, (de Celis et al., 1996; Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996)], decreased in the developing wing appendage (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1F-I and citations to published research (de Celis et al., 1996; Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996).

claim: Dpp activity levels decreased in the developing wing appendage upon dpp-RNAi expression.
source: As expected, dpp mRNA levels and Dpp activity levels, visualised with an antibody against the phosphorylated form of the Dpp transducer MAD (p-MAD) and by the expression of the Dpp target genes spalt and optomotor-blind [omb, (de Celis et al., 1996; Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996)], decreased in the developing wing appendage (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1F-I and citations to published research (de Celis et al., 1996; Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996).

claim: Brinker was de-repressed in all wing pouch cells upon dpp-RNAi expression.
source: Brinker (Brk), a transcription factor whose expression is repressed by the activity of Dpp and restricted to the lateral sides of the wing disc (Campbell and Tomlinson, 1999; Jaźwińska et al., 1999; Minami et al., 1999), was de-repressed in all wing pouch cells (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1G-I and citations to published research (Campbell and Tomlinson, 1999; Jaźwińska et al., 1999; Minami et al., 1999).

claim: Depletion in pupal stages had a mild impact on final wing size.
source: Depletion in pupal stages, when Dpp is expressed along the presumptive vein regions (de Celis, 1997; Yu et al., 1996), had a mild impact on final wing size (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2B,C and citations to published research (de Celis, 1997; Yu et al., 1996).

claim: The earlier the initiation of dpp-RNAi expression in larval wing primordia, the stronger the effects on wing size.
source: The earlier the initiation of Gal4-dependent expression of the dpp-RNAi hairpin in larval wing primordia, the stronger the effects on wing size (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The effects on tissue size increased in a gradual manner with earlier dpp depletion.
source: Remarkably, the effects on tissue size increased in a gradual manner.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Cell size was largely unaffected in dpp-depleted wings.
source: As expected, cell size was largely unaffected in dpp-depleted wings (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: dpp depletion gave rise to a reduction in both the width and length of the wing resulting in smaller but largely well-proportioned adult structures.
source: In all cases, we observed that dpp depletion gave rise to a reduction in both the width and length of the wing resulting in smaller but largely well-proportioned adult structures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The distal hinge structures were well formed and grown in dpp-depleted wings.
source: The distal hinge structures were well formed and grown.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: At longer exposures to dpp depletion, the size of the A compartment was reduced to a larger extent than the size of the P compartment.
source: At longer exposures, the size of the A compartment was reduced to a larger extent than the size of the P compartment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: dpp expression in wing cells is continuously required since the wing appendage is being specified and during the whole third instar stage to promote proliferative growth of the wing blade.
source: All together, these observations indicate that dpp expression in wing cells is continuously required since the wing appendage is being specified and during the whole third instar stage to promote proliferative growth of the wing blade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: p-MAD levels and Brk repression in the central part of the wing pouch were the first to be altered upon induction of dpp-RNAi expression.
source: p-MAD levels and Brk repression in the central part of the wing pouch were the first to be altered upon induction of dpp-RNAi expression (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: After 12 hr of dpp-RNAi induction, p-MAD levels were visibly reduced, and Brk initiated expression in the central part of the wing pouch.
source: After 12 hr of induction, p-MAD levels were visibly reduced, and Brk initiated expression in the central part of the wing pouch.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Twenty-four hours of dpp-RNAi induction were sufficient to completely remove p-MAD levels and obtain robust expression of Brk in all wing pouch cells.
source: Twenty-four hours of induction were sufficient to completely remove p-MAD levels and obtain robust expression of Brk in all wing pouch cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Longer exposures (at least 36 hr) to dpp-RNAi expression were required to remove the expression of the Dpp target genes Spalt and Omb from wing pouch cells.
source: Longer exposures (at least 36 hr) to dpp-RNAi expression were required to remove the expression of the Dpp target genes Spalt and Omb from wing pouch cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The wing pouch levels of Brk and p-MAD proteins are highly sensitive to reductions in Dpp.
source: These results indicate that the wing pouch levels of Brk and p-MAD proteins are highly sensitive to reductions in Dpp, and that Spalt and Omb either require stronger or longer reduction in Dpp activity levels or they are highly stable proteins, which might contribute to the robustness of Dpp-mediated patterning of the wing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spalt and Omb either require stronger or longer reduction in Dpp activity levels or they are highly stable proteins.
source: These results indicate that the wing pouch levels of Brk and p-MAD proteins are highly sensitive to reductions in Dpp, and that Spalt and Omb either require stronger or longer reduction in Dpp activity levels or they are highly stable proteins, which might contribute to the robustness of Dpp-mediated patterning of the wing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Adult wings expressing dpp-RNAi under the control of dpp-gal4 could not be recovered due to early pupal lethality.
source: Unfortunately, adult wings expressing dpp-RNAi under the control of dpp-gal4 could not be recovered due to early pupal lethality.
evidence: This is an experimental observation described in the text.

claim: The effects on the size of the wing pouch and of the whole wing disc were already observed after 24 hr of dpp-RNAi expression at the AP boundary.
source: The effects on the size of the wing pouch and of the whole wing disc were already observed after 24 hr of dpp-RNAi expression and longer exposures gave rise to a gradual reduction in wing pouch and wing disc size (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Longer exposures to dpp-RNAi expression at the AP boundary gave rise to a gradual reduction in wing pouch and wing disc size.
source: The effects on the size of the wing pouch and of the whole wing disc were already observed after 24 hr of dpp-RNAi expression and longer exposures gave rise to a gradual reduction in wing pouch and wing disc size (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The impact on the size of the wing pouch was stronger than on the size of the whole wing disc upon dpp depletion at the AP boundary.
source: The impact on the size of the wing pouch was stronger than on the size of the whole wing disc, thereby indicating that Dpp plays a major role in promoting the growth of the wing appendage and a minor role in the growth of the body wall (see below).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference from the data.

claim: Dpp plays a major role in promoting the growth of the wing appendage and a minor role in the growth of the body wall.
source: The impact on the size of the wing pouch was stronger than on the size of the whole wing disc, thereby indicating that Dpp plays a major role in promoting the growth of the wing appendage and a minor role in the growth of the body wall (see below).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The overall proportions of the wing pouch (width versus length) were largely unaffected by dpp depletion at the AP boundary.
source: The overall proportions of the wing pouch (width versus length, Figure 3 and Figure 4A,B) and the width of the wing hinge (the distance between the IR and the OR, Figure 3, Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) were largely unaffected by dpp depletion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3, Figure 4A,B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The width of the wing hinge was largely unaffected by dpp depletion at the AP boundary.
source: The overall proportions of the wing pouch (width versus length, Figure 3 and Figure 4A,B) and the width of the wing hinge (the distance between the IR and the OR, Figure 3, Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) were largely unaffected by dpp depletion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Temporally controlled expression of dpp-RNAi with ptc-gal4 caused a stronger reduction of the wing pouch than of the wing disc.
source: Temporally controlled expression of dpp-RNAi with ptc-gal4, which is restricted to the AP compartment boundary, also caused a stronger reduction of the wing pouch than of the wing disc (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 18°C, the size of the wing pouch and the wing disc was unaffected in dpp-RNAi-carrying discs.
source: In all cases, at 18°C, the size of the wing pouch and the wing disc was unaffected in dpp-RNAi-carrying discs.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: The wing pouch of control wing discs expressing GFP showed an eleven-fold increase in size during the first half of the third instar.
source: The wing pouch of control wing discs expressing GFP showed an eleven-fold increase in size during the first half of the third instar but only a two-fold increase during the last 24 hr of larval development (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The wing pouch of control wing discs expressing GFP showed only a two-fold increase during the last 24 hr of larval development.
source: The wing pouch of control wing discs expressing GFP showed an eleven-fold increase in size during the first half of the third instar but only a two-fold increase during the last 24 hr of larval development (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The impact of Dpp depletion on the size of the wing pouch and wing disc was still observed during the later developmental period.
source: Interestingly, the impact of Dpp depletion on the size of the wing pouch and wing disc was still observed during this later developmental period (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Dpp is required for wing pouch growth throughout the third instar larval period.
source: These results reinforce the requirement of Dpp for wing pouch growth throughout the third instar larval period (Figure 2) and suggest that the minor impact on wing pouch size observed in the first protocol upon 12-h depletion of Dpp (Figure 4A,B) should be explained by insufficient reduction of dpp mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dpp is a target of Hedgehog (Hh) coming from the P compartment.
source: Dpp is a target of Hedgehog (Hh) coming from the P compartment (Capdevila et al., 1994; Zecca et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research (Capdevila et al., 1994; Zecca et al., 1995).

claim: In mature third instar wing discs, Dpp is expressed in a narrow stripe at the AP boundary.
source: In mature third instar wing discs, Dpp is expressed in a narrow stripe at the AP boundary.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about Dpp expression.

claim: In young third instar discs, the Dpp stripe has a similar width but it proportionally occupies one third of the disc.
source: In young third instar discs, the Dpp stripe has a similar width but it proportionally occupies one third of the disc (Weigmann and Cohen, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Weigmann and Cohen, 1999).

claim: Cells lose expression of Dpp when they are displaced out of range of the Hh signal by growth of the disc.
source: Thus, cells lose expression of Dpp when they are displaced out of range of the Hh signal by growth of the disc.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biology of Dpp and Hh signaling.

claim: Transient exposure of cells to short hairpins can reduce gene function in their descendants, due to the high stability of these hairpins.
source: It has recently been shown that transient exposure of cells to short hairpins can reduce gene function in their descendants, due to the high stability of these hairpins (Bosch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research (Bosch et al., 2016).

claim: The longer the induction of dpp-RNAi, the broader the domain labelled by EGFP in G-TRACE experiments.
source: As expected, the longer the induction, the broader the domain labelled by EGFP, thereby reinforcing the notion that cells lose Dpp expression when they are displaced out of range of the Hh signal by growth of the disc (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: In the case of induction periods of 24 hr or 36 hr, the EGFP-labelled domain occupied a small fraction of the central region of the wing primordium, and the non-autonomous effects on tissue size were significant.
source: In the case of induction periods of 24 hr or 36 hr, this domain occupied a small fraction of the central region of the wing primordium, and the non-autonomous effects on tissue size were significant, visualised by the impact on the size of the P compartment and on the size of the A compartment not labelled by EGFP (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Dpp emanating from the AP compartment boundary is the one required to induce wing growth since the wing is being specified.
source: Although it is still possible that some low level of Dpp made outside the stripe might be knocked down in our experiments, our G-TRACE and temperature shifts results (Figures 4, 5 and 6) support the proposal that Dpp emanating from the AP compartment boundary is the one required to induce wing growth since the wing is being specified.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Incomplete reductions in the levels of dpp mRNA at the AP compartment boundary can have a clear impact on the size of the wing pouch.
source: Our experimental observation that incomplete reductions in the levels of dpp mRNA at the AP compartment boundary (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) can have a clear impact on the size of the wing pouch (Figure 4) is in conflict with the previously proposed role of low levels of non-boundary Dpp as the ones promoting wing growth (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015), and it strongly suggests that wing growth requires high levels of boundary Dpp.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4.

claim: Wing growth requires high levels of boundary Dpp.
source: Our experimental observation that incomplete reductions in the levels of dpp mRNA at the AP compartment boundary (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) can have a clear impact on the size of the wing pouch (Figure 4) is in conflict with the previously proposed role of low levels of non-boundary Dpp as the ones promoting wing growth (Akiyama and Gibson, 2015), and it strongly suggests that wing growth requires high levels of boundary Dpp.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The impact on the size of the A compartment of the wing pouch was stronger than on the size of the P compartment upon dpp depletion.
source: The impact on the size of the A compartment of the wing pouch was stronger than on the size of the P compartment (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The ratio between the EGFP and RFP expression domains was reduced in dpp-depleted wing discs when compared to controls and did not increase over time.
source: The ratio between the EGFP and RFP expression domains, a proxy of the expansion of the medial region, was reduced in dpp-depleted wing discs when compared to controls and did not increase over time (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Within the A compartment of the wing pouch, the size of the EGFP-expressing domain was reduced to a similar extent than the size of the domain not expressing EGFP.
source: Within the A compartment of the wing pouch, we observed that the size of the EGFP-expressing domain was reduced to a similar extent than the size of the domain not expressing EGFP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Dpp is equally required for the growth of both medial and lateral regions of the developing wing appendage.
source: These results suggest that Dpp is equally required for the growth of both medial and lateral regions of the developing wing appendage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In dpp-depleted wing discs, the size of the clones and the number of cells per clone in the wing pouch was significantly smaller than in EGFP-RNAi-expressing discs.
source: In dpp-depleted wing discs, the size of the clones and the number of cells per clone in the wing pouch was, as expected, significantly smaller than the size of clones quantified in the wing pouch of EGFP-RNAi-expressing discs (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The size reduction of posterior clones was slightly less than the one observed in anterior clones upon dpp depletion.
source: The size reduction of posterior clones was slightly less than the one observed in anterior clones (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both medial and lateral clones were smaller to a similar extent upon dpp depletion.
source: Both medial and lateral clones were smaller to a similar extent, thus reinforcing the notion that Dpp is equally required for the growth of both medial and lateral regions of the developing wing pouch (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The elongated shape of the clones along the proximal-distal axis of the wing pouch was largely unaffected by depletion of dpp.
source: We observed that the elongated shape of the clones along the proximal-distal axis of the wing pouch was largely unaffected by depletion of dpp (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The size of clones of cells in the body wall and hinge regions of dpp-depleted wing discs was reduced to a smaller extent than those located in the wing pouch.
source: The size of clones of cells in the body wall and hinge regions of dpp-depleted wing discs was reduced to a smaller extent than those located in the wing pouch (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dpp depletion caused a similar reduction in the size distribution of clones located in medial and lateral regions of the pupal wing.
source: Interestingly, Dpp depletion caused a similar reduction in the size distribution of clones located in medial and lateral regions of the wing (Figure 7E,F,F').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7E,F,F'.

claim: The size distribution of clones was nearly identical in medial and lateral regions of both control and dpp-depleted pupal wings.
source: We also observed that the size distribution of clones was nearly identical in medial and lateral regions of both control and dpp-depleted pupal wings (Figure 7E,F,F').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7E,F,F'.

claim: Temporally controlled depletion of Dpp gives rise to smaller but largely well-proportioned adult wings.
